extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in U.S. legal and political history
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedic article summarizing the Sedition Act of 1918: its legislative history, scope (amendments to the Espionage Act), enforcement, notable prosecutions, constitutional challenges, and repeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded scope of the Espionage Act (1918 amendments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sedition Act of 1918 was an Act of Congress that extended the Espionage Act of 1917 to cover a broader range of offenses, notably speech and the expression of opinion that cast the government or the war effort in a negative light or interfered with the sale of government bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though commonly called the Sedition Act, it was a set of amendments to the Espionage Act; many studies treat the Espionage and Sedition provisions together (for example, 'some fifteen hundred prosecutions were carried out under the Espionage and Sedition Acts, resulting in more than a thousand convictions'). Court decisions use the legal term Espionage Act whether as originally enacted or as amended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited language standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The law forbade the use of "disloyal, profane, scurrilous, or abusive language" about the United States government, its flag, or its armed forces, or language that caused others to view the American government or its institutions with contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This substantive phrasing defined punishable speech under the statute and was the basis for prosecutions of speakers and publishers; enforcement led to convictions of high-profile figures and activists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mail censorship authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The act allowed the Postmaster General to refuse to deliver mail that met those same standards for punishable speech or opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Postmaster General's authority to block mail was an effective tool for censoring printed materials and silencing activists; used alongside criminal prosecutions to suppress dissenting publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal applicability — wartime limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute applied only 'when the United States is in war' (it was enacted while the U.S. was in a declared state of war during World War I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because it was framed as a wartime measure, the provisions were tied to the period of hostilities; the amendments were set to expire in 1921 and the Sedition Act provisions were repealed on December 13, 1920 as part of sweeping postwar repeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties and sentencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Those convicted under the act generally received sentences of imprisonment for five to 20 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentences were substantial; some sentences were later commuted or mitigated (e.g., President Harding commuted Eugene V. Debs' sentence to time served; Wilson offered clemency to many convicted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement discretion and geographic variance
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. Attorneys initially had considerable discretion in using these laws; enforcement varied greatly between jurisdictions, with most activity in Western states where the Industrial Workers of the World was active.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement practices changed over time (Attorney General Gregory later instructed U.S. Attorneys not to act without his approval). Examples of prosecutions include Eugene V. Debs, Mollie Steimer, Marie Equi, and William C. Edenborn, illustrating both geographic and political variation in application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial treatment and constitutional challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Supreme Court upheld the Sedition Act in Abrams v. United States (1919) as applied to people urging curtailment of production of essential war materiel; Oliver Wendell Holmes' dissent articulated the 'marketplace of ideas' concept. Subsequent decisions, such as Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969), make similar legislation unlikely to be considered constitutional today.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jurisprudential trajectory shows an early deference to wartime restrictions on speech followed by a later, more protective free-speech standard; this evolution is central to assessing the constitutionality of comparable laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political context and attempts at peacetime sedition laws
rubrics_metrics.description: After the war, officials (notably Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer) advocated for a peacetime version of the Sedition Act; Congress considered many proposed versions but took no action. The Alien Registration Act of 1940 later became the first American peacetime sedition-style statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This context explains how wartime measures influenced later legislative proposals and the political debates over civil liberties versus national security in peacetime.
